title: Your first OCaml program
body: An OCaml source file is a sequence of definitions. The line `let () = print_endline "Hello, OCaml"` defines a value whose pattern is `()`, the single value of type `unit`, so evaluating the right-hand side runs the print as a side effect when the program starts.

You can try expressions interactively in `ocaml` (or `utop`) and you can compile a file with `ocamlfind ocamlopt main.ml -o main`. The toplevel prints each result with its type, such as `- : int = 4`; a compiled program prints only what you tell it to print.

Check that the file compiles before you reason about its output. Type errors are reported at compile time, with a line and column, and OCaml refuses to produce a program until every expression has a consistent type.
code:
let () = print_endline "Hello, OCaml"
let () = print_endline ("2 + 2 = " ^ string_of_int (2 + 2))
challenge: Add a third line that prints your own greeting followed by the length of that greeting, using String.length.
question: What does `let () = print_endline "x"` define?
correct: A unit-valued binding that runs the print when the module is evaluated
wrong: A function named print that you can call later
reasoning: The pattern () matches the unit value, so the definition exists only to evaluate its right-hand side for its effect.

title: Names are immutable: let and shadowing
body: `let x = 5` gives the name `x` to a value. It does not create a variable that can be assigned later. Reusing the same name with `let x = x + 1` creates a new, different binding that hides the old one from then on; the old value is unchanged.
`let ... in ...` limits a binding to one expression. In `let y = 2 in y * y` the name `y` exists only to the right of `in`, which keeps helper values from leaking into the rest of the file.
When a result surprises you, ask which binding a name refers to at that point. Shadowing is legal and common, but a closure created earlier still sees the value that was in scope when it was written.
code:
let x = 5
let add_x n = n + x
let x = 100
let () = Printf.printf "%d %d\n" x (add_x 1)
let area = let side = 4 in side * side
let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" area
challenge: Define `base = 10`, a function `scale n = n * base`, then shadow `base` with 1000 and print `scale 2`. Predict the number before you run it.
solution:
let base = 10
let scale n = n * base
let base = 1000
let () = Printf.printf "%d %d\n" base (scale 2)
question: After `let x = 5`, `let f n = n + x`, `let x = 100`, what is `f 1`?
correct: 6, because f captured the first x
wrong: A type error, because x is defined twice
reasoning: Shadowing adds a new binding; it never mutates the earlier one, so closures keep the value they captured.

title: Basic types and separate operators
body: The core types are `int`, `float`, `bool`, `char`, `string` and `unit`. OCaml never converts between them silently: `1 + 2.0` is a type error. Convert explicitly with `float_of_int`, `int_of_float` and `string_of_int`.

Arithmetic operators are typed. `+ - * /` work on `int`, while `+. -. *. /.` work on `float`. Strings join with `^`. Integer division truncates toward zero and `mod` gives the remainder, so `7 / 2` is `3` and `(-7) mod 2` is `-1`.
Comparisons such as `=` and `<` are polymorphic structural comparisons and require both sides to have the same type. Use `==` only when you really mean physical identity, which is rare.
challenge: Compute the average of the integers 3, 4 and 8 as a float printed with two decimals, converting before dividing.
question: Why does `1 + 2.5` fail to compile?
correct: `+` works on int only and OCaml does not convert automatically; use `+.` with floats
wrong: OCaml needs a semicolon between the operands
Floats cannot be added to anything
reasoning: Operators are typed per number kind, and implicit conversion would hide precision loss, so the compiler asks you to be explicit.

title: Functions: definition, application and fun
body: A function is a value. `let square x = x * x` is shorthand for `let square = fun x -> x * x`. You apply it by writing the argument after the name with no parentheses: `square 5`. Parentheses only group, as in `square (2 + 3)`.

Application binds tighter than any operator, so `square 2 + 3` means `(square 2) + 3`. A function with several parameters is written `let add x y = x + y` and called `add 1 2`; the next stage explains why that is really a chain of one-argument functions.
Functions that do not have a name are written with `fun`. They are used as arguments, for example `List.map (fun n -> n * 2) [1; 2; 3]`. Prefer a named function when the body is longer than one line.
challenge: Write `cube` and print `cube 3`, then print `cube (1 + 1)` to see how parentheses change the argument.
solution:
let cube x = x * x * x
let () = Printf.printf "%d %d\n" (cube 3) (cube (1 + 1))
question: How does OCaml read `square 2 + 3`?
correct: As `(square 2) + 3`, because application binds tighter than `+`
wrong: As a syntax error without parentheses
reasoning: Function application is the tightest-binding construct, so only explicit parentheses extend the argument.

title: if as an expression and Printf formats
body: `if` is an expression: both branches must have the same type and the whole `if` has that type. There is no statement form, so `let sign = if n < 0 then "negative" else "non-negative"` is the normal way to choose a value.

`Printf.printf` takes a format string whose conversions are checked against the arguments at compile time. `%d` is an int, `%s` a string, `%f` a float, `%c` a char and `%b` a bool; writing `%d` for a string is a type error, not a runtime crash.
An `if` without `else` must produce `unit`. When you see a type error about `unit`, check that you did not leave out the `else` branch of an expression that should return a value.
expectedStdout:
-2 is negative
0 is zero
5 is positive
ocaml has 5 chars, ratio 0.5
challenge: Write `fizz n` that returns "fizz" when n is divisible by 3 and the number as a string otherwise, then print it for 1 to 6 on one line.
question: What must be true of the two branches of `if c then a else b`?
correct: `a` and `b` must have the same type, which is the type of the whole expression
wrong: Only the then-branch is type checked
reasoning: An if expression produces one value, so the compiler needs a single type for it regardless of which branch runs.
